turst.aura: One dreadful but human-shaped Swiss spectral huntsman Türst, selecting Rickenbach GREEN hunting dress. Adult stern man in green coat and old hat sounding a curved hunting horn with one normal hand; other hand relaxed. Stormy Lucerne farm landscape in winter before Epiphany, open barn doorway behind and windblown clouds. No dogs pictured; distinctive three-legged or hybrid anatomy belongs to accompanying pack, not Türst, and MUST NOT be put on him. Ominous supernatural Wild Hunt atmosphere, normal ears and two human legs.

basis_claims.quote: is a legendary folkloric figure from the agricultural communities of Lucerne, dating to the pre-Christian era. He is described as a "dreadful huntsman", of whom people should be wary in stormy weather. Türst blows his hunting horn through villages in the tempestuous months preceding Epiphany, accompanied by a baying pack of three-legged hunting dogs.

statement.id: Türst adalah tokoh cerita rakyat dari komunitas petani Luzern yang berasal dari masa pra-Kristen, digambarkan sebagai "pemburu mengerikan" yang harus diwaspadai saat cuaca berbadai; ia meniup terompet berburu menembus desa-desa pada bulan-bulan berbadai menjelang Epifani bersama kawanan anjing berkaki tiga.
statement.en: Türst is a folk figure of Lucerne's farming communities dating to pre-Christian times, a 'dreadful huntsman' to beware of in stormy weather, who blows his horn through villages in the stormy months before Epiphany with a pack of three-legged hounds.

basis_claims.quote: He appears in a green hunting costume in Rickenbach, accompanied by a pack of animals which are half dog and half pig. In Wolhusen, to avoid Türst, the citizens erected crosses. If a cross were to fall, the farmers would have bad luck until the cross stood straight again. The local people of Pilatus say that Türst is a ghost and a "dreadful huntsman"

statement.id: Di Rickenbach ia tampil berpakaian berburu hijau dengan kawanan setengah anjing setengah babi; di Wolhusen warga mendirikan salib untuk menghindarinya, dan bila salib roboh petani akan sial sampai salib ditegakkan; warga Pilatus menyebutnya hantu dan "pemburu mengerikan".
statement.en: In Rickenbach he appears in green hunting dress with a half-dog, half-pig pack; in Wolhusen people raised crosses against him, and a fallen cross brought farmers bad luck until set upright; the people of Pilatus call him a ghost and a 'dreadful huntsman'.

basis_claims.quote: Der Türst (auch Dürst genannt) ist eine Sagenfigur aus dem Luzerner Hinterland, die noch aus heidnischen Zeiten stammt. Er wird als „höllischer Jäger“ bezeichnet

statement.id: Türst (juga disebut Dürst) adalah tokoh legenda dari pedalaman Luzern yang berasal dari masa kafir dan disebut "pemburu neraka".
statement.en: Türst (also called Dürst) is a legendary figure from the Lucerne hinterland dating from heathen times, called the 'hellish huntsman'.

basis_claims.quote: It is also said that barn doors should stay open at this time, enabling Türst to hunt through the barn unhindered. Sträggele, his wife, appears in some Türst legends. Other legends say that Türst terrifies dairy cows, causing them to sicken and cease their milk production.

statement.id: Konon pintu lumbung harus dibiarkan terbuka pada masa itu agar Türst dapat berburu menembus lumbung tanpa halangan; istrinya Sträggele muncul dalam sebagian legenda, dan legenda lain menyebut ia menakuti sapi perah hingga sakit dan berhenti menghasilkan susu.
statement.en: Barn doors should be left open at this time so Türst can hunt through unhindered; his wife Sträggele appears in some legends, and others say he terrifies dairy cows until they sicken and stop giving milk.

basis_claims.quote: "the dwarfs had taken shape first and acquired life in the flesh of Ymir and were then maggots, but by decision of the gods they became conscious with intelligence and had the shape of men though they live in the earth and in rocks. Modsognir was a dwarf and the second was Durinn."

statement.id: Menurut Snorri dalam Gylfaginning 14, para kurcaci mula-mula terbentuk dan hidup di daging Ymir sebagai belatung, lalu atas keputusan para dewa memperoleh kesadaran, akal, dan rupa manusia walau tinggal di tanah dan bebatuan; Modsognir kurcaci pertama dan Durinn yang kedua.
statement.en: Per Snorri in Gylfaginning 14, the dwarfs first took shape and life in Ymir's flesh as maggots, then by the gods' decision gained awareness, intelligence and human shape though living in earth and rocks; Modsognir was a dwarf and the second was Durinn.

basis_claims.quote: According to Völuspà 9, the dwarfs were created by ginnheilög goð, "the high holy gods", who resolved to fashion them "out of Brimir's blood and Blainn's bones," a phrase typically interpreted to mean the blood and flesh of the primordial giant, Ymir.

statement.id: Menurut Völuspá 9, para kurcaci diciptakan "dewa-dewa yang mahasuci" yang memutuskan membentuk mereka "dari darah Brimir dan tulang Blainn", ungkapan yang biasa ditafsirkan sebagai darah dan daging raksasa purba Ymir.
statement.en: According to Völuspá 9, the dwarfs were made by 'the high holy gods', who resolved to shape them 'out of Brimir's blood and Blainn's bones', usually read as the blood and flesh of the primordial giant Ymir.

basis_claims.quote: Modsognir, auch Motsognir (altnordisch Módsognir bzw. Mótsognir), ist in der nordischen Mythologie der erste Zwerg und wurde von den Göttern erschaffen. Umstritten ist die Bedeutung des Namens, am ehesten könnte man ihn mit ‚der Müde, der Kraftlose‘ wiedergeben

statement.id: Modsognir atau Motsognir adalah kurcaci pertama dalam mitologi Nordik yang diciptakan para dewa; arti namanya diperdebatkan, paling mungkin "yang lelah, yang tak bertenaga".
statement.en: Modsognir or Motsognir is the first dwarf in Norse mythology, created by the gods; the meaning of the name is disputed, most likely 'the weary, powerless one'.

nonhuman_features: No anatomical deformation claimed; principal dwarf in documented human-shaped post-origin stage.
motsognir.historical_basis: Mótsognir ('he who drinks in might'), also Móðsognir in the Hauksbók variant ('he who drinks in courage'), is ruler of the dwarfs; Völuspá 10 calls him 'lord of all the dwarves'. Per Snorri in Gylfaginning 14, the dwarfs first took shape and life in Ymir's flesh as maggots, then by the gods' decision gained awareness, intelligence and human shape though living in earth and rocks; Modsognir was a dwarf and the second was Durinn. According to Völuspá 9, the dwarfs were made by 'the high holy gods', who resolved to shape them 'out of Brimir's blood and Blainn's bones', usually read as the blood and flesh of the primordial giant Ymir. Modsognir or Motsognir is the first dwarf in Norse mythology, created by the gods; the meaning of the name is disputed, most likely 'the weary, powerless one'.

additional_sources.title: Gylfaginning, Origin of the Dwarfs, section 15; I. A. Blackwell translation
additional_sources.evidence: The primary account states the dwarf race first were maggots, then received human shape and understanding. Immediately identifies Modsognir and Durin as principal dwarfs; quoted Voluspa verse says dwarfs were formed like men. This portrait selects their documented human-shaped stage, with no personal larval-transformation assertion.

visual_requirements: Goethe literary bearded crowned forest spirit

erlking.aura: One sinister human-shaped elderly forest elf-king from Goethe's literary Erlkönig, long beard and simple crown atop white hair, wearing a modest long archaic cloak, reaching one ordinary hand from among dark alder trunks. Full solitary figure contained within picture, no child or traveller visible. Silent deeply unsettling predatory woodland mood from night, mist and facial expression. Ordinary rounded human ears, no tree-bark body, antlers, wings or animal anatomy. A literary supernatural king portrait rather than a literal alder-tree hybrid.

basis_claims.quote: In European folklore and myth, the Erlking is a sinister elf who lingers in the woods. He stalks children who stay in the woods for too long and kills them with a single touch.

statement.id: Dalam cerita rakyat dan mitos Eropa, Erlking adalah elf jahat yang berdiam di hutan, mengintai anak-anak yang terlalu lama di hutan, dan membunuh mereka dengan sekali sentuh.
statement.en: In European folklore and myth the Erlking is a sinister elf lingering in the woods, stalking children who stay too long and killing them with a single touch.

basis_claims.quote: is a name used in German Romanticism for the figure of a spirit or "king of the fairies". It is usually assumed that the name is a derivation from the ellekonge (older elverkonge, i.e. "Elf-king") in Danish folklore.

statement.id: Nama Erlking (Erlkönig, "raja pohon alder") dipakai dalam Romantisisme Jerman untuk roh atau "raja para peri" dan umumnya dianggap turunan dari ellekonge (lebih tua: elverkonge, "raja elf") dalam cerita rakyat Denmark.
statement.en: The name Erlking (Erlkönig, 'alder-king') was used in German Romanticism for a spirit or 'king of the fairies' and is usually thought to derive from Danish folklore's ellekonge (older elverkonge, 'elf-king').

basis_claims.quote: The name was first used by Johann Gottfried Herder in his ballad Erlkönigs Tochter (1778), an adaptation of the Danish folk ballad Hr. Oluf han rider (1739), and was taken up by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe in his poem Erlkönig (1782), which was set to music by Schubert and others. Goethe added a new meaning, as "Erl" means not "elf" but "black alder"

statement.id: Nama ini pertama dipakai Johann Gottfried Herder dalam balada Erlkönigs Tochter (1778), saduran balada rakyat Denmark Hr. Oluf han rider (1739), lalu diambil Goethe dalam puisi Erlkönig (1782) yang digubah Schubert dan lainnya; Goethe menambah makna baru karena "Erl" berarti "alder hitam", bukan "elf".
statement.en: The name was first used by Johann Gottfried Herder in Erlkönigs Tochter (1778), adapted from the Danish ballad Hr. Oluf han rider (1739), then taken up by Goethe in Erlkönig (1782), set by Schubert and others; Goethe added a new sense, 'Erl' meaning 'black alder', not 'elf'.

nonhuman_features: No anatomical deformation claimed; sinister supernatural king among alder trees.
erlking.historical_basis: In European folklore and myth the Erlking is a sinister elf lingering in the woods, stalking children who stay too long and killing them with a single touch. The name Erlking (Erlkönig, 'alder-king') was used in German Romanticism for a spirit or 'king of the fairies' and is usually thought to derive from Danish folklore's ellekonge (older elverkonge, 'elf-king'). The name was first used by Johann Gottfried Herder in Erlkönigs Tochter (1778), adapted from the Danish ballad Hr. Oluf han rider (1739), then taken up by Goethe in Erlkönig (1782), set by Schubert and others; Goethe added a new sense, 'Erl' meaning 'black alder', not 'elf'.

clurichaun.aura: One six-inch-tall old male Irish cellar fairy Naggeneen, with a wrinkled human face LIKE a withered apple, wearing modest old little red-toned garments as illustration, perched beside a wine cask drinking from a tiny cup. Huge cask bung and ordinary wine-bottle silhouette establish miniature scale. Normal human anatomy and rounded ears, never a literal apple head. Uncanny mischievous wine-cellar mood, candlelight against damp deep stone.

basis_claims.quote: is a mischievous fairy in Irish folklore known for his great love of drinking and a tendency to haunt breweries, pubs and wine cellars. He is related to the leprechaun and has sometimes been conflated with him as a shoemaker and a guardian of hidden treasure. This has led some folklorists to suppose that the clurichaun is merely a leprechaun on a drinking spree

statement.id: Clurichaun (clúrachán, Irlandia/Irish clobhair-ceann) peri jahil cerita rakyat Irlandia (Irish folklore), gemar minum, menghantui gudang anggur; kerabat leprechaun; di Irlandia.
statement.en: The clurichaun (clúrachán, Irish clobhair-ceann) is a mischievous fairy of Irish folklore who loves drink and haunts cellars; related to the leprechaun.

basis_claims.quote: Like the leprechaun, the clurichaun is a solitary fairy, encountered alone rather than in groups, as distinct from the trooping fairies.

statement.id: Seperti leprechaun, clurichaun peri penyendiri.
statement.en: Like the leprechaun, the clurichaun is a solitary fairy.

basis_claims.quote: In the folktale "The Haunted Cellar", recorded by Thomas Crofton Croker in 1825, a clurichaun named Naggeneen haunts the wine cellar of an Irish lord, drinking everything in sight and playing frightening pranks on the servants. He is described as a little man measuring 6 in (150 mm) tall, with a face like a withered apple.

statement.id: Dalam The Haunted Cellar (Croker, Thomas Crofton Croker, 1825), Naggeneen menghantui gudang anggur bangsawan Irlandia (Irish), setinggi 15 cm, wajah seperti apel layu; topi merah, gesper perak.
statement.en: In The Haunted Cellar (Thomas Crofton Croker, 1825), Naggeneen haunts an Irish lord's cellar, 6 in tall, face like a withered apple.

nonhuman_features: No anatomical deformation claimed; six-inch supernatural wine-cellar haunter, withered-apple face simile retained as wrinkles.
clurichaun.historical_basis: The clurichaun (clúrachán, Irish clobhair-ceann) is a mischievous fairy of Irish folklore who loves drink and haunts cellars; related to the leprechaun. Like the leprechaun, the clurichaun is a solitary fairy. In The Haunted Cellar (Thomas Crofton Croker, 1825), Naggeneen haunts an Irish lord's cellar, 6 in tall, face like a withered apple.

onryo.aura: One human-shaped resentful spirit of Sugawara no Michizane in a restrained historically informed Heian Japanese court robe and black eboshi cap, stern scholarly adult male face, standing alone before distant palace roofs under a violent thunderstorm. Entire human body retained, two coherent human hands, normal face, no corpse deformation, horns, animal legs or modern horror woman costume. Ominous disaster-bearing spirit conveyed through storm and spectral moonlit atmosphere. No attack, victims or other deity. A spirit-stage portrait before later Tenjin worship; robe details illustrative.

basis_claims.quote: In ancient Japan, the spirits of the dead who died with resentment, called goryō 御霊 or onryō 怨霊, were thought to cast curses.

statement.id: Di Jepang kuno, onryō ialah arwah orang yang wafat dengan dendam dan dipercaya dapat mengutuk.
statement.en: In ancient Japan, onryō were spirits of the resentful dead believed to cast curses.

basis_claims.quote: Spirits thought to cause plague, natural disaster, or other such large-scale calamities were feared as onryō, and people tried to console and pacify them.

statement.id: Onryō ditakuti sebagai penyebab wabah dan bencana besar; orang berusaha menenangkan mereka.
statement.en: Onryō were feared as causes of plague and disasters and were pacified.

basis_claims.quote: Michizane was a distinguished scholar, poet, and statesman who died in exile, having been slandered by enemies at court.

statement.id: Michizane adalah cendekiawan dan pejabat yang meninggal dalam pengasingan.
statement.en: Michizane was a scholar and statesman who died in exile.

basis_claims.quote: After his death, a series of extraordinary natural disasters and plagues caused the untimely deaths of his detractors. In an attempt to appease his vengeful spirit, he was posthumously pardoned and promoted to high office, but the disasters continued.

statement.id: Menurut legenda, bencana dan wabah mengikuti kematiannya; ia diampuni dan dinaikkan pangkat untuk menenangkan rohnya, namun bencana berlanjut.
statement.en: In legend disasters and plagues followed his death; he was pardoned and promoted to appease his spirit, but calamities continued.

basis_claims.quote: dedicated to Sugawara Michizane (845–903). Michizane was a distinguished scholar

statement.id: Kisah ini berhubungan dengan Sugawara Michizane.
statement.en: The account concerns Sugawara Michizane.

nonhuman_features: No anatomical deformation claimed; resentful dead court scholar associated with curses and disaster after exile.
onryo.historical_basis: In ancient Japan, onryō were spirits of the resentful dead believed to cast curses. Onryō were feared as causes of plague and disasters and were pacified. Michizane was a scholar and statesman who died in exile. In legend disasters and plagues followed his death; he was pardoned and promoted to appease his spirit, but calamities continued. The account concerns Sugawara Michizane.

ameonna.aura: One mature human-shaped Japanese rain woman based on Toriyama Sekien: rain-soaked long dark hair, plain wet modest kimono fully covering body, standing in heavy night rain and visibly licking the back of one raised ordinary human hand. Other normal hand relaxed, coherent five-finger anatomy. Old Japanese courtyard bamboo and dark foliage backdrop, supernatural rain atmosphere conveyed by downpour and somber stillness. Human face with visible tongue lightly touching hand, no extra mouth, horns, webbed limbs or child-snatching narrative.

basis_claims.quote: Ameonna (雨(あめ)女(おんな), "rain woman") is a Japanese yōkai thought to call forth rain, illustrated in Toriyama Sekien's Konjaku Hyakki Shūi as a woman standing in the rain and licking her hand.

statement.id: Ameonna berarti perempuan hujan dan Sekien menggambarkannya di tengah hujan.
statement.en: Ameonna means rain woman and Sekien depicts her in rain.

basis_claims.quote: You’ll find her first in Toriyama Sekien’s book, Konjaku Hyakki Shūi, supplement to the 100 demons from the present and past. In it is a black and white depiction of a rain-soaked woman, very creepily licking her hand.

statement.id: Gambar Sekien menunjukkan perempuan basah yang menjilat tangannya.
statement.en: Sekien pictures a rain-soaked woman licking her hand.

basis_claims.quote: It is said that the divine woman of Mount Wu in ancient China becomes a cloud in the morning and rain in the evening. I wonder if Ame-onna is also this kind of being.

statement.id: Keterangan Sekien membandingkan ameonna dengan perempuan ilahi Gunung Wu.
statement.en: Sekien compares ameonna with the divine woman of Mount Wu.

nonhuman_features: No anatomical deformation claimed; supernatural rain woman performing documented hand-licking gesture.
ameonna.historical_basis: Ameonna means rain woman and Sekien depicts her in rain. Sekien pictures a rain-soaked woman licking her hand. Sekien compares ameonna with the divine woman of Mount Wu.
artistic_changes: Exact facial likeness, clothing folds, compositional details and painterly lighting are illustrative; no anatomical deformation asserted beyond selected documented account.

oshiroibaba.aura: One bent-backed elderly female Japanese yokai of Totsukawa, combining documented old-woman appearance and recorded visual accessories: heavy messy WHITE FACE POWDER with wrinkles still visible, modest old kimono, one hand supporting a worn paper umbrella, other hand with a walking cane, sake flask tied at waist. A small old mirror is tied to a loose trailing cord dragging behind her on the village lane, visibly separate from her anatomy. Entire figure and mirror inside image. Uncanny solitary nighttime village atmosphere, no floating head, extra limbs, horns or deformed face invented.

basis_claims.quote: is a yōkai old woman from the Totsukawa river in Yoshino District, Nara Prefecture.

statement.id: Oshiroibabā adalah yōkai perempuan tua dari daerah Totsukawa di Nara.
statement.en: Oshiroibabā is an old-woman yōkai from the Totsukawa area of Nara.

basis_claims.quote: The oshiroibabā is said to be a yōkai in the form of an old woman who appears while dragging a mirror and making a jingling sound.

statement.id: Ia menyeret cermin dengan suara gemerincing.
statement.en: She drags a mirror with a jingling sound.

basis_claims.quote: Toriyama Sekien's Konjaku Hyakki Shūi depicts an old woman with a very bent back, wearing a large broken umbrella on her head, holding a walking stick with her right hand and a tokkuri (flask for sake) in her left hand, under the name of oshiroibabā.

statement.id: Sekien menggambarkannya membungkuk dengan payung, tongkat, dan botol sake.
statement.en: Sekien depicts her bent-backed with an umbrella, cane and sake flask.

basis_claims.quote: Their most defining feature is their wrinkly old face caked with thick, sloppy, white face powder.

statement.id: Uraian belakangan menekankan riasan putih tebal yang berantakan.
statement.en: A later description emphasizes thick, messy white makeup.

nonhuman_features: No anatomical deformation claimed; old-woman yokai with thick messy white makeup and jingling dragged mirror.
oshiroibaba.historical_basis: Oshiroibabā is an old-woman yōkai from the Totsukawa area of Nara. She drags a mirror with a jingling sound. Sekien depicts her bent-backed with an umbrella, cane and sake flask. A later description emphasizes thick, messy white makeup.

far-darrig.aura: One short approximately two-and-a-half-foot elderly Irish fairy in RED cap and RED coat, deeply wrinkled but human face, sitting alone beside the best place at a rural hearth with a sly unsettling expression and one ordinary hand held toward warmth. Tiny scale indicated by large hearth stones and normal-size empty wooden chair. Ordinary rounded human ears and human limbs. Nickname Rat Boys is NOT anatomical evidence: no rat snout, furred paws or tail. Quiet eerie prankster mood, no changeling infant or gore.

basis_claims.quote: A far darrig or fear dearg is a faerie type in Irish mythology. The name far darrig is an Anglophone pronunciation of the Irish words fear dearg, meaning Red Man, as the far darrig is said to wear a red coat and cap. They are sometimes known as Rat Boys as they are said to be rather fat, have dark, hairy skin, long snouts and skinny tails.

statement.id: Far darrig (fear dearg) peri mitologi Irlandia (Irish), Lelaki Merah (Red Man), bermantel dan bertopi merah; juga Rat Boys; di Irlandia. Pelafalan Anglophone.
statement.en: The far darrig (fear dearg) is an Irish fairy, Red Man, in a red coat and cap; also called Rat Boys.

basis_claims.quote: The far derrig is generally described as short, while sometimes described as tall. It's said the far derrig has the ability to change sizes. An 1832 description from T. Crofton Croaker in Munster says the far derrig are around 2.5 feet tall with a wrinkled face, long grey hair, and a sugarloaf hat.

statement.id: Pendek atau tinggi, dapat mengubah ukuran; T. Crofton Croker (Croaker), Munster, 1832: tinggi sekitar 2,5 kaki, wajah keriput.
statement.en: Short or tall, can change size; T. Crofton Croker, Munster, 1832: about 2.5 feet, wrinkled face.

basis_claims.quote: The Far Darrig (fear dearg), which means the Red Man, for he wears a red cap and coat, busies himself with practical joking, especially with gruesome joking.

statement.id: Yeats: Far Darrig (fear dearg), Red Man, bertopi dan bermantel merah, sibuk dengan lelucon keji; W. B. Yeats.
statement.en: Yeats: the Far Darrig (fear dearg), Red Man, in red cap and coat, busies himself with gruesome practical joking.

basis_claims.quote: On dit de lui qu'il a tendance à forcer les habitants d'une maison à l'accueillir chez eux, et à lui réserver la meilleure place, au coin du feu.

statement.id: Ia memaksa penghuni rumah menerimanya dan memberinya tempat terbaik dekat perapian (coin du feu).
statement.en: He forces householders to take him in and give him the best place by the fire (coin du feu).

nonhuman_features: No anatomical deformation claimed; size-changing solitary fairy represented in short red-clad form.
far-darrig.historical_basis: The far darrig (fear dearg) is an Irish fairy, Red Man, in a red coat and cap; also called Rat Boys. Short or tall, can change size; T. Crofton Croker, Munster, 1832: about 2.5 feet, wrinkled face. Yeats: the Far Darrig (fear dearg), Red Man, in red cap and coat, busies himself with gruesome practical joking. He forces householders to take him in and give him the best place by the fire (coin du feu).

Coherent source-supported anatomy and identifying features

hodekin.aura: One small human-shaped German castle house spirit Hödekin, an old sober-faced male in humble archaic clothes and a LITTLE FELT PILEUS CAP, sitting silently at the threshold of a bishop's medieval stone castle kitchen at night. Normal human face, rounded ears and human limbs, both hands visible. The tiny felt hat identifies him; eerie watchful house-spirit aura conveyed by empty kitchen, dim hearth and long shadow. No violent scene, blood, toads, horns or animal anatomy.

basis_claims.quote: Hödekin (variously spelled Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin , and Hütchen , etc.) is a kobold (house spirit) of German folklore. The name, a diminutive meaning "Little Hat", refers to the pileus hat he wears

statement.id: Hödekin (juga Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin, dan Hütchen) adalah kobold (roh rumah) dalam cerita rakyat Jerman; namanya bentuk kecil yang berarti "Topi Kecil", merujuk topi pileus yang dikenakannya.
statement.en: Hödekin (also Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin and Hütchen) is a kobold (house spirit) of German folklore; the name, a diminutive meaning 'Little Hat', refers to the pileus cap he wears.

basis_claims.quote: Hödekin is known for haunting the castle of Bishop Bernard (Bernhardus), Prince-Bishopric of Hildesheim, located in Lower Saxony. In some versions of the legend, the spirit inhabits Winzenburg, a county which he helped the bishopric obtain.

statement.id: Hödekin dikenal menghantui kastel Uskup Bernhard (Bernhardus) dari Keuskupan-Pangeran Hildesheim di Niedersachsen; dalam sebagian versi ia menghuni Winzenburg, wilayah yang dibantunya diperoleh keuskupan.
statement.en: Hödekin is known for haunting the castle of Bishop Bernard (Bernhardus) of the Prince-Bishopric of Hildesheim in Lower Saxony; in some versions he inhabits Winzenburg, a county he helped the bishopric obtain.

basis_claims.quote: Der Hödeken ist der Burggeist der Winzenburg. Er wird als eine zwergenartige Gestalt beschrieben (Kobold), die auch als Bote zwischen Hildesheim und Winzenburg Nachrichten übermittelte. Der Weg zwischen Winzenburg und Hildesheimer Domhof, den Hödeken nach dem Tod des letzten Grafen von Winzenburg entlanggeeilt sein soll, um die Todesnachricht zu überbringen, wird „Rennstieg“ genannt.

statement.id: Hödeken adalah roh kastel Winzenburg, sosok mirip kurcaci (kobold) yang juga menjadi pembawa pesan antara Hildesheim dan Winzenburg; jalan antara Winzenburg dan Domhof Hildesheim yang konon dilaluinya untuk mengabarkan kematian Graf Winzenburg terakhir disebut "Rennstieg".
statement.en: Hödeken is the castle spirit of Winzenburg, a dwarf-like figure (kobold) who also carried messages between Hildesheim and Winzenburg; the road between Winzenburg and Hildesheim's Domhof that he reputedly ran to report the last count of Winzenburg's death is called the 'Rennstieg'.

basis_claims.quote: Der Hödeken war ein Geist, der sich am Hof des Bischofs von Hildesheim aufhielt. Er hinderte die Nachtwachen am Einschlafen, gab dem Bischof militärische Ratschläge und warnte ihn vor kommenden Gefahren. Gelegentlich half er auch anderen Hildesheimern. Einmal bat jemand den Hödeken, seine Frau während seiner Abwesenheit zu beschützen.

statement.id: Menurut Grimm bersaudara, Hödeken adalah roh di istana Uskup Hildesheim yang mencegah penjaga malam tertidur, memberi uskup nasihat perang, memperingatkannya akan bahaya, kadang menolong warga Hildesheim lain, dan pernah diminta menjaga istri seseorang selama suaminya pergi.
statement.en: Per the Brothers Grimm, Hödeken was a spirit at the court of the Bishop of Hildesheim who kept the night watch awake, gave the bishop military advice, warned him of dangers, sometimes helped other townsfolk, and was once asked to guard a man's wife in his absence.

basis_claims.quote: „[…] auf dem Haupt trug er einen kleinen Filzhut, wovon man ihm den Namen Hütchen auf Niedersächsisch Hödeken gegeben hatte.“

statement.id: Menurut Grimm bersaudara, ia memakai topi laken kecil di kepalanya, sehingga diberi nama Hütchen, dalam bahasa Saxon Rendah Hödeken.
statement.en: Per the Grimms, he wore a little felt hat, whence the name Hütchen, in Low Saxon Hödeken.

nonhuman_features: No anatomical deformation claimed; dwarf-like house spirit wearing the defining little felt hat.
hodekin.historical_basis: Hödekin (also Hödeken, Hütgin, Hüdekin and Hütchen) is a kobold (house spirit) of German folklore; the name, a diminutive meaning 'Little Hat', refers to the pileus cap he wears. Hödekin is known for haunting the castle of Bishop Bernard (Bernhardus) of the Prince-Bishopric of Hildesheim in Lower Saxony; in some versions he inhabits Winzenburg, a county he helped the bishopric obtain. Hödeken is the castle spirit of Winzenburg, a dwarf-like figure (kobold) who also carried messages between Hildesheim and Winzenburg; the road between Winzenburg and Hildesheim's Domhof that he reputedly ran to report the last count of Winzenburg's death is called the 'Rennstieg'.
